title: Where it grows
subtitle: From Bordeaux to warmer places
objectives: Explain why warm climates suit it
Explain its role in Bordeaux today

steps.title: Bordeaux
steps.body: Petit Verdot is mainly a Left Bank grape, used in small amounts in the Médoc. Château Margaux and others use a few percent. Plantings fell in the 20th century, but warmer vintages since the 1990s have helped it ripen more reliably, and some estates have added more.
steps.highlight: A small part of Left Bank blends

steps.title: Warmer homes
steps.body: In warm, dry places, Petit Verdot ripens fully. Spain grows it in La Mancha and Castilla, sometimes as a single variety. Australia's Riverland and McLaren Vale, California, Virginia and Washington all make varietal Petit Verdot. Argentina and Chile use it in blends.

steps.prompt: Why does Petit Verdot do better in warm climates?
options: It needs a lot of rain
steps.explanation: As a late ripener, it needs a long, warm season to reach full ripeness.

steps.title: Climate change
steps.body: With warmer vintages, Petit Verdot is gaining interest in Bordeaux as a grape that keeps acidity in heat. Growers value its freshness and colour as other grapes ripen faster. It's one reason some see it as part of Bordeaux's future blend.

steps.prompt: Petit Verdot is mainly a Right Bank grape in Bordeaux.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's mostly found in small amounts on the Left Bank, in the Médoc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Petit Verdot is a minor Left Bank blending grape
Warm regions in Spain, Australia and the US ripen it fully
Climate change has renewed interest in Bordeaux
